About: Coulomb's Law

Source

Model
F = kq₁q₂/r² with k = 8.987551×10⁹ N·m²/C²; macro charges ±10 µC over ±5 cm (1 mm snap); atomic charges ±10e (e = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C, the exact SI value) over ±50 pm (1 pm snap).
Concept
Charge quantisation and Coulomb's law. Charge comes only in whole-number multiples of e (q = ne); the electrostatic force between two such charges is proportional to each charge and to the inverse square of their separation, attractive for opposite signs and repulsive for like signs.
Serves
Quantisation, the inverse-square law and Newton's third law in one picture, at two scales: the same formula governs µC charges centimetres apart and whole numbers of elementary charges picometres apart — ten orders of magnitude in distance. The atomic-scale sliders step by exactly one e, so q = ne is enforced, not asserted.
Inquiry
Double the separation — what happens to the force? And when the charges are unequal, which one feels the stronger pull?
Misconception
That the bigger charge pulls harder. It cannot: the two forces are an action–reaction pair, always exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, whatever q₁ and q₂ are.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict: double the distance

Two charges, −4 µC and +8 µC, sit 3 cm apart and attract with F ≈ 320 N. They are moved to 6 cm apart — double the separation. What happens to the force?

2 · Feel the inverse square

The charges are −4 µC and +8 µC. Compare the force arrows at 3 cm with the arrows at 6 cm, and then at the closest separation the spheres allow. How does the change in arrow length compare with the change in separation?

3 · Predict: unequal charges

Now the charges are unequal: q₁ = −2 µC, q₂ = +8 µC — four times bigger. Which charge feels the stronger pull?

4 · Equal and opposite, always

q₁ = −2 µC and q₂ = +1 µC. Raise q₂ towards +10 µC, then make q₁ positive as well. Compare the two arrows at every setting: does either charge ever pull harder than the other?

5 · Quantisation, and the same law a billion times smaller

These charges are −2e and +4e, forty picometres apart. Charge is quantised: it exists only in whole-number multiples of the elementary charge, q = n e with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so these are exactly two and four electrons' worth and nothing in between. The same F = kq₁q₂/r² now reads 1.15 × 10⁻⁶ N — one law from tabletop µC to the charges inside an atom.

The Physics

Coulomb’s Law · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two small charged spheres sit on a line, and each is held in place by a person. The sim lets you change the size and sign of each charge and the distance between them, and it shows the force that each charge feels.

What you'll learn

  • How the sign of two charges decides whether they push apart or pull together.
  • How the force between two point charges depends on the size of each charge and on the distance between them.
  • How the same law works for microcoulombs and centimetres and for elementary charges and picometres.
The apparatus: two charges on a line, a ruler beneath, and the separation r between them.

What's on screen

  • The two charges: coloured spheres with a + or − sign, each labelled with its value.
  • Force arrows: one arrow on each charge, with a label that gives its size in newtons.
  • Separation bar above the charges, reading "separation r", and a ruler below.
  • Readouts in the sidebar: the force |F|, the separation r and the kind of interaction.
See itStart with the opening scene: −4 µC and +8 µC, 3 cm apart. Watch for: the two spheres and the bar reading separation r = 3.0 cm.

03

Like charges repel, unlike charges attract

Charge comes in two kinds, written + and −. Two charges of the same sign are called like charges, and they push each other apart. Two charges of opposite sign pull each other together. The force acts along the straight line that joins the two charges.

In the sim the arrow on each charge shows which way that charge is pushed or pulled, and the readout names the interaction. Arrows pointing away from the other charge mean repulsion. Arrows pointing towards it mean attraction. The product q₁q₂ is positive for a like pair and negative for an unlike pair, which is the sign test the sim uses.

The two people in the picture lean to match. In attraction each one hauls back on a rope. In repulsion each one pushes in on the sphere.

See itTake −4 µC and +8 µC, an unlike pair. Watch for: the readout attraction (opposite signs), and arrows pointing toward the other charge.
04

Coulomb's law gives the force as kq₁q₂/r²

For two point charges at rest, the size of the force on each one is

F = k |q₁q₂| / r², k = 8.987551 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²
The force grows with each charge and falls as the separation grows. The distance enters squared.

The charges must be in coulombs and r in metres to give newtons. The opening scene has q₁ = −4 µC, q₂ = +8 µC and r = 3 cm. Then F = 8.987551 × 10⁹ × (4 × 10⁻⁶)(8 × 10⁻⁶) / (0.03)² = 320 N, as the readout shows.

Note the unit conversions: 4 µC is 4 × 10⁻⁶ C and 3 cm is 0.03 m. Leaving either in the sim's display units gives a wrong answer by a large power of ten.

See itStart from the opening pair, 3 cm apart. Watch for: |F| 320 N in the readouts and on both force labels.
05

Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter

Because r is squared, doubling r divides F by 2² = 4, and halving r multiplies F by 4. The charges stay the same.

r (cm)F for −4 µC and +8 µC (N)Arrow, as a fraction of 400 N
1.51278off scale, capped
33200.80
679.90.20

The force arrow has a length proportional to F, and a full-length arrow stands for 400 N. At 3 cm the arrow is 80 % of full length, and at 6 cm it is 20 %. At 1.5 cm the force is above 400 N, so the sim draws the arrow at full length and says it is capped. The label still gives the true value.

See itMove the same two charges to 6 cm apart. Watch for: |F| 79.9 N, with the arrows only a fifth of full length.
06

The two forces are equal and opposite

Each charge pushes or pulls on the other. The force of q₂ on q₁ and the force of q₁ on q₂ form an action and reaction pair, as Newton's third law requires, so they have the same size and opposite directions. The formula agrees, because it treats q₁ and q₂ in the same way.

A larger charge does not pull harder. Take q₁ = −2 µC and q₂ = +8 µC, 3 cm apart. Then F = 8.987551 × 10⁹ × (2 × 10⁻⁶)(8 × 10⁻⁶) / (0.03)² = 160 N. Both labels read 160 N, even though q₂ is four times q₁.

The two charges do not accelerate in the sim because each person holds one in place. Free charges would have unequal accelerations if their masses differed, but the forces would still be equal.

See itSet q₁ = −2 µC and q₂ = +8 µC at 3 cm. Watch for: force on q₁ = 160 N and force on q₂ = 160 N, with the two arrows of the same length.
07

Charge comes in whole multiples of e

Charge is quantised. Every charge is a whole number n of the elementary charge, q = ne, with e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. There is nothing between one e and the next. The Atomic scale shows this: its slider moves in whole units of e only.

The same law applies at this scale. Take q₁ = −2e and q₂ = +4e, 40 pm apart. In coulombs the charges are −3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and +6.41 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and r = 40 × 10⁻¹² m. Then F = 8.987551 × 10⁹ × (3.204 × 10⁻¹⁹)(6.409 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (4 × 10⁻¹¹)² = 1.15 × 10⁻⁶ N.

That is about 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ of the 320 N at the Macro scale. The charges and the distance are both tiny, yet the formula is the same.

See itSwitch to the Atomic scale with −2e and +4e, 40 pm apart. Watch for: |F| 1.15 × 10⁻⁶ N, and under each charge its value as n × e in coulombs.
08

Where it matters

  • Atoms and molecules. The pull between a nucleus and its electrons is a Coulomb force, and it holds atoms together and underlies chemical bonding.
  • Static cling and sparks. Rubbed objects hold small imbalances of charge, and Coulomb forces make hair stand up and paper stick.
  • Ionic crystals. In table salt, the attraction between + and − ions, at the spacing of the lattice, holds the crystal together.
  • Electric fields. The force on a charge q is written F = qE, and Coulomb's law gives the field E of a point charge. Gauss's law builds on it.
09

Summary

In one line. Two point charges push or pull along the line joining them, with a force set by the sizes of the charges and by how far apart they are.

Key points

  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract: q₁q₂ > 0 is repulsion, q₁q₂ < 0 is attraction.
  • F = k|q₁q₂|/r², with k = 8.987551 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², so doubling r divides F by 4.
  • The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, whatever the charges.
  • Charge is q = ne, and the same law holds from centimetres to picometres.

Common mix-ups

  • "The bigger charge pulls harder." Both forces in the pair have the same size.
  • "Doubling the distance halves the force." The distance is squared, so the force falls to a quarter.
  • "Charge can have any value." Charge comes only in whole multiples of e.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict F for −4 µC and +8 µC at 4 cm, then drag a charge to check.
  • Make q₁ positive with q₂ and watch the arrows reverse and the readout change.
  • On the Atomic scale, find a separation at which F is about 10⁻⁶ N for −2e and +4e.
